company: Prosus N.V. (forced seller of Delivery H
bull_thesis: The bull case is that the event resolved well and the market still has not paid for what is left behind. Prosus, the Amsterdam-listed technology holding company, was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink its 26.5% stake in Delivery Hero, the German food-delivery group, as the price of being allowed to buy Just Eat Takeaway.com for 4.1 billion euros. Management executed that mandated sale about as well as a forced sale can be executed: 4.5% of Delivery Hero to Uber at 20 euros a share on 17 April 2026, then 5% to Aspex Management of Hong Kong at 22 euros on 11 May 2026, and finally, on 16 July 2026, a binding, non-withdrawable promise to tender the residual 16.8% into Uber's 41.50-euro cash takeover offer - roughly double what Prosus accepted three months earlier and about 2.8 times Delivery Hero's 52-week low of 14.80 euros. The forced seller is finished, and it sold at premiums rather than into a fire sale. What is left is the real security, and on the company's own published numbers it is cheap. Prosus discloses its asset value daily; as of 31 July 2026 it stands at 158.1 billion US dollars, or 65.20 euros per share, against today's 41.29-euro price - a 37% discount. Roughly 51.30 euros per share of that is a single liquid holding, about 22.8% of Tencent, the Chinese internet group, so a buyer at 41.29 euros pays 0.80 times the marked value of the Tencent stake alone and collects the 32.8 billion dollars of unlisted businesses and 7.7 billion dollars of other listed holdings for nothing. Meanwhile the company retires its own stock relentlessly - close to 42 billion dollars returned since June 2022, about 30% of the free float, and still running at roughly 100 million euros a week (2,527,143 shares bought between 6 and 10 July 2026 at an average of 39.5574 euros) - which lifts value per share by arithmetic every day the discount stays wide. The operating businesses have stopped being a drag: the year to 31 March 2026 delivered about 12% revenue growth, ecosystem adjusted operating earnings up roughly 44%, free cash flow above 1.5 billion dollars, and profitability across all three regional ecosystems for the first time. The near-term tape has also turned: Tencent has climbed from HK$443 on 27 July to HK$490.40 today, reclaiming its 50-day average near HK$449.50, and Prosus has followed from 37.85 to 41.29 euros. If Tencent recovers toward its 200-day average near HK$534.50 and the discount narrows toward 30%, the shares are worth about 49 euros; on today's asset value at a 30% discount, about 45.60. Morgan Stanley, upgrading the stock on 25 March 2026, set a 51-euro target on the argument that the discount had reached the top of its range. The conditions the bull case needs are simply stated: Chinese internet sentiment stabilises, Tencent's 12 August 2026 second-quarter results do not disappoint, and management keeps buying stock at a third off.
bear_thesis: The bear case has two parts, and the first is fatal to the reason this name sits in an event-driven book at all. The forced selling was in Delivery Hero shares, not in Prosus shares, so there was never a supply overhang on this security to clear - and the residual position is far too small to move the price in any case. Prosus carries its remaining 16.8% Delivery Hero stake at 2.2 billion dollars, about 1.9 billion euros; spread across roughly 2.11 billion Prosus shares that is about 0.91 euro per Prosus share, some 2.2% of the price and 1.4% of asset value. The part not yet earned, the gap between Delivery Hero's 37.35 euros today and the 41.50-euro offer, is worth about 0.10 euro per Prosus share, and it does not arrive until the second half of 2027, subject to merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances and to Germany's financial regulator first approving the offer document, which has not yet happened. A quarter of one percent of the share price, more than a year out, with regulatory conditions attached, is not a special situation. Second, and more seriously, the thing that actually moves this security has no floor under it. Three-quarters of the value is one Chinese equity. Tencent trades at HK$490.40 against a 52-week high of HK$683, still 28% below that high and below its 200-day average of about HK$534.50, with a 52-week low of HK$411 set this year. Prosus mirrors it: 41.29 euros against a 52-week high of 63.94 and a low of 36.17 set within the past two weeks. The floor our board recorded, 37.365, was traded through on the way down - a level the security has already broken is not a floor, it is a recent price - and there is no tender, no cash consideration, no deal price obliging anyone to pay a number here. The support is a mark-to-market on a volatile foreign equity. If Tencent returns to its 52-week low, roughly 8 euros a share of value disappears and Prosus can trade to the mid-30s without the discount widening at all, and Tencent's next scheduled test is 12 August 2026. Third, and specific to today, the trade has got worse precisely because it worked. A week ago the shares were 37.85 euros and our board's 46.21-euro target implied 22% of upside. After a 9% rally driven entirely by Tencent - the discount barely moved, from about 38% to about 37% - that upside is roughly 12% against a modelled downside near 16%. The asymmetry has inverted while nothing about the underwriting changed. Finally, the holding-company discount is structural and has never durably closed, and the street cannot even agree it is wide: Morgan Stanley upgraded four months ago because the discount was at the top of its range, while Goldman Sachs initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a 41-euro target - a level now reached - calling the discount 30% against a 40% historical average, that is, narrow rather than wide. Goldman's specific concern also bites: weaker cash flow from the operating businesses could force Prosus to keep selling Tencent shares to fund the buyback, shrinking the very asset that provides the backing. There is also a small negative option outstanding: the European Commission's compliance deadline is 11 October 2026 while the Uber deal does not close until the second half of 2027, and no Brussels decision accepting a 2027 settlement against a 2026 obligation has been published.
sop_bull: About 46 to 49 euros per share. Start from the company's own published asset value on 31 July 2026: a 164.9 billion dollar gross portfolio less 6.8 billion dollars of net debt equals 158.1 billion dollars, or 65.20 euros per share on roughly 2.11 billion shares. The bull path does not require a higher mark on the parts - it requires the gap between price and parts to close part-way. Two levers: the discount narrowing from 37% toward the 30% that prevailed before this year's China selloff, which on today's asset value alone is worth about 45.60 euros a share; and Tencent recovering from HK$490.40 toward its 200-day average near HK$534.50, which lifts asset value per share to roughly 69.80 euros and, at a 30% discount, gives about 48.90. The buyback adds independently: roughly 5 billion dollars a year of repurchase at a 37% discount adds about 3 to 4% to value per share annually, and the July disclosures confirm it is running at scale. Morgan Stanley's 51-euro target (25 March 2026) sits just above this range; our board's 46.21-euro target sits inside it, at an implied discount of about 29%. The Delivery Hero resolution contributes about 0.10 euro of unearned spread - immaterial, and deliberately not leaned on.
sop_bear: About 34 to 35 euros per share, and the honest answer is that this is a modelled bear value, not a verified floor. The parts, per the company's 31 July 2026 disclosure and a dollar-euro rate of about 1.15: Tencent 124.4 billion dollars (about 51.30 euros per share), other listed holdings 7.7 billion (about 3.18 euros, of which Delivery Hero is 2.2 billion dollars or about 0.91 euro), unlisted businesses 32.8 billion (about 13.52 euros), less 6.8 billion dollars of net debt (about 2.80 euros). The adverse case marks Tencent back to its 52-week low of HK$411, about 16% below today - a retest of a level already seen this year rather than a crisis assumption - which removes roughly 8 euros a share, and haircuts the unlisted book by a fifth for the same emerging-market risk aversion, removing another 2.70 euros. That takes value per share to roughly 54.50 euros, and holding the discount at its current 37% gives about 34.30. The first waypoint on the way down is the 52-week low of 36.17 euros set in the past two weeks. Nothing contractual arrests the decline: there is no cash tender, no deal price, no net-cash backstop - net debt is 6.8 billion dollars, small at about 4% of the portfolio but still a liability rather than a cushion. The only genuine hard support is that Tencent alone is marked at 51.30 euros per share, so a buyer at 41.29 already owns the rest for free; that is asset backing, and it moves with the tape.
sop_fair_value: About 42 euros per share, probability-weighted; the parts themselves are worth 65.20 euros per share (Prosus's own published figure, 31 July 2026) and the gap is the persistent holding-company discount.
sop_breakdown: Per Prosus share, on roughly 2.11 billion shares and the company's 31 July 2026 disclosure (158.1 billion dollars equals 137.5 billion euros, so about 1.15 dollars to the euro): Tencent, about 22.8% of the Chinese internet group, 124.4 billion dollars, about 51.30 euros - 75% of asset value. Other listed holdings 7.7 billion dollars, about 3.18 euros, comprising Meituan 2.3 billion, Delivery Hero 2.2 billion (about 0.91 euro per Prosus share, the entire remaining position), Swiggy 1.7 billion and smaller holdings. Unlisted businesses 32.8 billion dollars, about 13.52 euros, split Europe 15.9 billion, Latin America 8.5 billion, India 4.7 billion, other 3.7 billion. Less net debt of 6.8 billion dollars, about 2.80 euros, being 10.1 billion of cash against 16.9 billion of debt. Net asset value 158.1 billion dollars, 65.20 euros per share, against a 41.29-euro price - a 37% discount. Reconciling to a base case: a 30% chance the discount narrows toward 30% as Chinese internet sentiment recovers, worth about 47 euros; a 50% chance the status quo holds - the discount stuck in the mid-to-high 30s, Tencent drifting around current levels, the buyback adding 3 to 4% a year to value per share - worth about 42 to 43 euros; a 20% chance Tencent retests its 52-week low with the discount unchanged, worth about 34.50 euros. Weighted, about 42 euros against a 41.29-euro price.
risk_reward: Roughly 0.7 to 1, and the risk is undefined. Upside to a 46-euro target is about +11%; downside to a 34.50-euro bear value is about -16%. Our board recorded 2.76 to 1, but that was computed from a live price of 39.72 and a floor of 37.365 - and both inputs have since been overtaken: the shares broke to 36.17 in late July and have since rallied to 41.29, so the floor was never a floor and the entry level is gone. The asymmetry has inverted in the past week purely through price, because the whole 9% move came from Tencent while the discount barely narrowed. More important than the arithmetic: on a genuine defined-risk special situation the downside is bounded by something contractual. Here it is bounded by nothing - the support is a daily mark on a Chinese equity 28% below its 52-week high - so the true loss distribution has a long left tail the ratio does not capture.
catalyst_status_note: Verified on 3 August 2026 from Prosus company announcements, the European Commission's August 2025 conditional clearance of the Just Eat Takeaway.com acquisition, and Uber's 16 July 2026 offer announcement. The regulator-mandated sell-down is complete in substance: 4.5% of Delivery Hero placed with Uber at 20 euros on 17 April 2026, 5% with Aspex Management at 22 euros on 11 May 2026, and on 16 July 2026 an irrevocable undertaking to tender the residual 16.8% into Uber's 41.50-euro cash offer, which takes Uber to about 53% of the economics. The forced selling was in Delivery Hero shares, never in Prosus shares, and the residual is carried at 2.2 billion dollars, about 0.91 euro per Prosus share. What remains unearned is the 11% gap between Delivery Hero's 37.35 euros today and the 41.50-euro offer, worth about 0.10 euro per Prosus share and settling in the second half of 2027 subject to merger-control clearance and to Germany's financial regulator approving the offer document, which has not yet been published. The event has fired; the residual spread is immaterial to this security.
catalyst_summary: The regulator-mandated Delivery Hero sell-down is finished and was never large enough to matter: Prosus cut 26.5% to 16.8% at premiums (20 euros to Uber on 17 April, 22 euros to Aspex on 11 May 2026) and on 16 July 2026 gave a binding promise to tender the rest into Uber's 41.50-euro cash offer, leaving about 0.10 euro per Prosus share of unearned spread that does not settle until the second half of 2027 - against a security whose price is set, three-quarters of it, by Tencent.
dated_milestone: Four dates are live, and none of them is a special-situation trigger for this security. 12 August 2026: Tencent reports second-quarter results - the only calendar item that reliably moves Prosus, and it belongs to another company and cuts both ways. 26 August 2026: Prosus's annual general meeting, a routine governance date. 11 October 2026: the European Commission's extended deadline for Prosus to have complied with its divestment commitment; the two-month extension was granted on 2 June 2026 after Naspers asked Brussels on 25 May 2026 to drop the forced sale altogether. Prosus's stated position, from its 16 July 2026 announcement, is that the sale to Uber is a fair price and an effective way to comply; whether the Commission formally accepts a settlement that completes in 2027 against a 2026 deadline is the one genuinely open item, and its downside is a small residual placement, not a re-rating. Second half of 2027: expected completion of Uber's voluntary cash takeover offer for Delivery Hero at 41.50 euros a share, announced 16 July 2026, conditional on a minimum acceptance of 50% plus one share (Prosus's binding undertaking takes Uber to about 53% of the economics, so this is effectively pre-satisfied) and on merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances, with Germany's financial regulator required to approve the offer document before the acceptance period can begin.
forcing_function: There is no longer one, and that is the finding. The event that was supposed to force the re-rating has resolved, and the resolution is worth about 0.10 euro per share on a 41.29-euro stock, arriving in the second half of 2027. The nearest hard date, 11 October 2026, is a compliance checkpoint on 1.4% of asset value, not a trigger. What remains that could plausibly force a re-rating is not an event but a process: the open-ended buyback, which retires stock at a 37% discount and has already taken about 30% of the free float out since June 2022 and is still running at roughly 100 million euros a week, and any further move to simplify the ownership structure between Prosus and its parent Naspers, which took a step forward with the recent share exchange. Neither has a date. Absent an event, the driver is Tencent's own tape, and Tencent's 12 August 2026 second-quarter results are the single scheduled item most likely to move this security - which is precisely the objection: the forcing function belongs to a company we do not own directly and would not underwrite in this book.
consensus_delta: There is no disagreement with the market worth owning here, and pretending otherwise is where this position would go wrong. The street's view is straightforward and, as far as we can verify, correct: Prosus is a discounted way to own Tencent, the discount is wide because Chinese internet sentiment has been poor, and the buyback is the main thing management controls. This week proved the point rather than refuting it. Between 27 July and today the shares rose about 9%, from 37.85 to 41.29 euros, while the discount to published asset value moved only from about 38% to about 37%. The entire move was Tencent going from HK$443 to HK$490.40. Nothing in the Delivery Hero situation changed. If you own this security you are expressing a view on Chinese internet equities, whatever label the position carries. On the analyst split: Morgan Stanley upgraded to overweight on 25 March 2026 with a 51-euro target, explicitly because the discount had widened to the top of its post-2022 range. Goldman Sachs then initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a 41-euro target - a level the shares have now reached - describing the discount as 30% against a 40% historical average, the opposite framing from a different asset-value methodology, and warning that weaker operating cash flow could force more Tencent selling to fund the buyback. When two houses cannot agree whether the discount is wide or narrow, 'the discount is at its extreme' is a methodology choice, not an edge. Where our board did disagree with the market was in treating the forced Delivery Hero sale as a live supply story on this security, and that disagreement does not survive verification. The selling was in another company's shares; the position was under 2% of asset value; it has been sold at premiums; and the residual is contracted at a fixed price. If any gap remains between our view and the market's it runs the other way - the market may still be crediting Prosus with Delivery Hero optionality that has already been converted into a fixed 41.50-euro claim settling in late 2027. The one asymmetry we would defend is arithmetic rather than analytical: at 41.29 euros a buyer pays 0.80 times the marked value of the Tencent stake alone and receives about 14 euros a share of other portfolio, net of debt, at no cost. That is a fact about the price, not a variant view - and it was equally true, at the same 0.80 ratio, when the stock was 37.85 euros a week ago.
valley_of_death: The next three to nine months carry real downside with no offsetting event. The dominant risk is simply Tencent, which is roughly 75% of asset value. It has rallied to HK$490.40 and reclaimed its 50-day average near HK$449.50, but it remains 28% below its 52-week high of HK$683 and below its 200-day average of about HK$534.50, and its 52-week low of HK$411 is only 16% away. The immediate test is 12 August 2026, when Tencent reports second-quarter results; the concerns going in are gaming revenue and the earnings drag from heavy artificial-intelligence investment spending, which has already trimmed 2026 and 2027 consensus earnings forecasts. A disappointing print takes Prosus down with it, and a return to the HK$411 low removes about 8 euros a share of value and puts the stock in the mid-30s on an unchanged discount. Second, the discount can widen independently of the assets, and each point costs roughly 0.65 euro a share. Third, currency: the portfolio is denominated in dollars and Hong Kong dollars while the listing is in euros, so a firmer euro mechanically lowers value per share. Fourth, the 11 October 2026 compliance deadline: if Brussels declines to treat the irrevocable undertaking to Uber as compliance, Prosus must place a residual Delivery Hero block into the market in the fourth quarter - immaterial to value at about 0.91 euro a share, but an unhelpful headline in a tape looking for reasons to sell. There is no cash-burn or maturity problem. Net debt is 6.8 billion dollars (10.1 billion of cash against 16.9 billion of debt) on a 164.9 billion dollar gross portfolio, roughly 4%; free cash flow was above 1.5 billion dollars in the year to March 2026; and 2027 maturities were refinanced with new bonds raised in July 2026. The near-term risk here is entirely price, not solvency.
positioning_washout: The mechanical selling in this situation was never in Prosus - it was in Delivery Hero, and it is over. Prosus placed 4.5% with Uber at 20 euros and 5% with Aspex at 22 euros, both at or above the prevailing market, and has now contracted the remaining 16.8% to Uber at 41.50 euros; there is no further Prosus supply coming to the Delivery Hero tape, and Delivery Hero has re-rated from a 52-week low of 14.80 euros to 37.35 against a 200-day average of 24.98. Whatever wash-out premium existed accrued to Delivery Hero's shareholders, not to ours. On Prosus's own register the flow runs the other way and is supportive rather than distressed: the company is the dominant buyer of its own stock, having retired about 30% of the free float and close to 42 billion dollars of value since June 2022, and it is still buying - 2,527,143 shares between 6 and 10 July 2026 at an average of 39.5574 euros, roughly 100 million euros in a single week, which is a meaningful share of daily volume. The recent share exchange with Naspers has also simplified the cross-holding that historically muddied the valuation. The genuine forced-selling risk today is exogenous: passive and emerging-market funds cutting Chinese internet exposure, which hits Tencent and Prosus together and is precisely the pressure that produced the 36.17-euro low two weeks ago. That is a live headwind on the position, not a set-up to buy into - and note that the wash-out low has already been bought, 14% ago, by whoever was willing to catch it.
moderator_conclusion: Pass for now - not because the company is bad, but because this is not the security the board thought it was buying, and because the past week has taken away what little compensation the setup offered. The event we underwrote has already happened, and it happened well. Prosus was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink a 26.5% stake in Delivery Hero as the condition of buying Just Eat Takeaway.com, and it did so at premiums: 20 euros to Uber on 17 April 2026, 22 euros to Aspex on 11 May, and then on 16 July a binding promise to tender the residual 16.8% into Uber's 41.50-euro cash offer. The forced seller is finished. The re-rating that flowed from it went to Delivery Hero's own shareholders, whose stock went from under 15 euros to 37.35. What reaches us is about 0.10 euro per Prosus share of unearned spread, settling in the second half of 2027 subject to regulatory clearance and to Germany's financial regulator approving an offer document that has not yet been published. That is a quarter of one percent of the share price. You cannot build a defined-risk position on it. The downside floor our board recorded at 37.365 never existed: the shares broke to 36.17 euros in late July. A level the security has already traded through is a recent price, not a floor, and there is nothing contractual beneath it - no tender, no deal price, no net cash. What actually sets the price is Tencent, three-quarters of asset value, and the last two weeks demonstrate it beyond argument: Tencent rose from HK$443 to HK$490.40, Prosus rose from 37.85 to 41.29 euros, and the discount barely moved. That is an uncapped exposure to Chinese internet equities wearing a special-situation label, and it does not belong in this book. The timing point is the one that decides it. A week ago the recorded target of 46.21 euros implied 22% of upside against a modelled bear case near 34 to 35; today the same target implies about 11% against the same downside. The trade got worse because it worked, and the rally was not our catalyst - we would have been paid for being right about Tencent, which is not what this funnel underwrites. The separate question is whether the security is cheap, and the honest answer is yes. Prosus's own disclosure on 31 July 2026 puts asset value at 158.1 billion dollars, or 65.20 euros a share, against a 41.29-euro price - a 37% discount. The Tencent stake alone is marked at about 51.30 euros a share, so a buyer pays 0.80 times one liquid holding and gets 32.8 billion dollars of unlisted businesses and the rest for nothing, while the company retires roughly 100 million euros of its own stock a week at that discount. The operating side has genuinely turned: about 12% revenue growth in the year to March 2026, ecosystem earnings up roughly 44%, free cash flow above 1.5 billion dollars, every ecosystem profitable. That is a real value case, and it is why the value score is a 3 rather than a 1 - there is substantial, liquid, daily-marked asset backing, but it marks to market on a volatile Chinese equity, so the margin of safety is genuine without being defined. It is held to a 3 rather than a 4 for three reasons: the street cannot agree the discount is even wide (Goldman Sachs, 4 June 2026, calls it 30% against a 40% historical average, and its 41-euro target has now been reached); the buyback that does the compounding may itself have to be funded by selling the asset that provides the backing; and the entry price is 9% worse than it was a fortnight ago for no change in the underwriting. Our judgement: hand this name to the value book and underwrite it there as a discounted holding company carrying China risk, sized for that. In the event-driven book, where the entry condition is a live, dated catalyst with a floor beneath it, it is a pass. The only development that would bring it back here is a concrete move to simplify the Prosus-Naspers ownership structure or a formal process against the discount - that would be the first genuine forcing event this security has had. Absent that, the next thing to happen is Tencent's second-quarter results on 12 August 2026, and taking a position into another company's earnings print is not a special situation either.
interrogator_dossier:
# PRX.AS — Prosus N.V. — Forensic Interrogation of the Event

*Event-driven special situation. Board label: forced seller / forced-divestment flow. Every fact below was re-checked against public sources on 3 August 2026, and the price and asset figures are as of today's session.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC — what the event was, and where it now stands

The trade our board wrote down was a supply story. Prosus, the Amsterdam-listed technology holding company, was ordered by Europe's competition regulator to shrink a large stake in Delivery Hero, the German food-delivery group. The European Commission made that sell-down a condition of letting Prosus buy Just Eat Takeaway.com for 4.1 billion euros, clearing the deal in August 2025 on the commitment that Prosus cut its 26.5% Delivery Hero holding to below 5% within twelve months of closing. The classic way to trade a forced seller is to wait until the seller is done, then buy the security once the mechanical pressure on the price has gone.

The first problem is definitional, and it is fatal to the trade as written. The forced selling was in Delivery Hero shares, not in Prosus shares. There was never an overhang on this security to clear.

The second problem is that the seller has finished, and finished well. The verified sequence:

| Date | Event | Price / terms | Residual stake |
|---|---|---|---|
| Aug 2025 | Commission clears the Just Eat Takeaway purchase, conditional on cutting the Delivery Hero holding below 5% within twelve months | — | 26.5% |
| 17 Apr 2026 | 13,582,342 shares (about 4.5% of Delivery Hero) sold to Uber | 20.00 euros per share | 21.8% |
| 11 May 2026 | 15,188,284 shares (about 5.0%) sold to Aspex Management of Hong Kong | 22.00 euros per share | 16.8% |
| 25 May 2026 | Naspers, Prosus's majority owner, asks Brussels to drop the forced-sale requirement altogether | — | 16.8% |
| 2 Jun 2026 | Commission refuses that, but extends the compliance deadline by two months, to 11 October 2026 | — | 16.8% |
| 16 Jul 2026 | Uber launches a voluntary cash takeover offer for all of Delivery Hero; Prosus gives an irrevocable undertaking (a binding, non-withdrawable promise) to tender its entire residual holding | 41.50 euros per share in cash, about 14.8 billion dollars of equity value; closing targeted for the second half of 2027 | 16.8%, contractually spoken for |

Two placements at premiums, then the balance handed to a strategic buyer at 41.50 euros — roughly double the 20 euros accepted three months earlier, and about 2.8 times Delivery Hero's 52-week low of 14.80 euros. The re-rating this produced went overwhelmingly to Delivery Hero's own shareholders: their stock trades at 37.35 euros today against a 200-day average of 24.98 and that 14.80 low.

The event has fired. It did not slip and it did not stall. It resolved, and it resolved competently.

## 2. THE LOAD-BEARING TEST — is the event real, dated, binding, and does it move *this* security?

Real: yes. Dated: two dates remain. Binding: yes — and that is precisely the problem, because a binding contract at a known price is a spread, and this spread is negligible.

The two remaining dates:

- **11 October 2026** — the extended deadline by which Prosus must have complied with its divestment commitment. Prosus's stated position, from the 16 July announcement, is that Uber's offer represents a fair price and an effective way to comply. Whether Brussels formally accepts a contract that settles in 2027 as satisfying a 2026 obligation is the one genuinely open item; as of today no Commission decision on that point has been published. Either way, the consequence of a negative answer is that Prosus places a small block of Delivery Hero shares with someone else — an administrative outcome, not a re-rating.
- **Second half of 2027** — expected completion of Uber's offer, conditional on a minimum acceptance of 50% plus one share (Prosus's undertaking takes Uber to roughly 53% of the economics, so that condition is effectively pre-satisfied), on merger-control and financial-regulatory clearances, and on Germany's financial regulator approving the offer document before the acceptance period can even begin. That approval had not been published as of today.

Now the size test, which is where the thesis dies. Prosus publishes the holding's mark daily: the residual Delivery Hero stake was carried at 2.2 billion dollars at 31 July 2026, about 1.9 billion euros. Spread across roughly 2.11 billion Prosus shares, the **entire remaining position is worth about 0.91 euro per Prosus share** — 2.2% of a 41.29-euro share price and 1.4% of stated asset value. The part not yet earned, the gap between Delivery Hero's 37.35 euros today and the 41.50-euro offer, is about **0.10 euro per Prosus share**, and it does not settle until the second half of 2027, with regulatory conditions attached.

Roughly a quarter of one percent of the share price, more than a year out. You cannot build a defined-risk position in an 88 billion euro holding company on that.

## 3. WHAT ACTUALLY SETS THE PRICE

Prosus publishes its own asset value daily. As of **31 July 2026** it stands at 158.1 billion dollars (137.5 billion euros), or **65.20 euros per share**:

| Component | Value ($bn) | Per Prosus share (euros) |
|---|---|---|
| Tencent, the Chinese internet group (about 22.8% of it) | 124.4 | ~51.30 |
| Other listed holdings — Meituan 2.3, Delivery Hero 2.2, Swiggy 1.7, smaller positions | 7.7 | ~3.18 |
| Unlisted portfolio — Europe 15.9, Latin America 8.5, India 4.7, other 3.7 | 32.8 | ~13.52 |
| Less net debt — 10.1 cash against 16.9 debt | (6.8) | ~(2.80) |
| **Net asset value** | **158.1** | **65.20** |

At today's 41.29 euros the shares trade at roughly a **37% discount** to that figure. Put another way: the Tencent stake alone is marked at about 51.30 euros per Prosus share, so a buyer at 41.29 euros pays **0.80 times one liquid holding** and collects the 32.8 billion dollar unlisted portfolio and the other listed assets for nothing.

Which means, to three-quarters of its value, this security is a discounted way to own Tencent — and Tencent is why the stock is where it is. The last week makes the point better than any argument could. On 27 July, when this name was last examined, Tencent traded at HK$443 and Prosus at 37.85 euros. Today Tencent is HK$490.40, up 3.2% in the session and up about 11% in a week, and Prosus is 41.29 euros, up 3.3% today and up about 9% over the same stretch. The discount barely moved — from about 38% to about 37%. Nothing about the Delivery Hero situation changed in that week. The entire move was Tencent.

Where that leaves the tape: Tencent has reclaimed its 50-day average (about HK$449.50) but sits well below its 200-day (about HK$534.50) and 28% below its 52-week high of HK$683, with a 52-week low of HK$411. Prosus mirrors it: 41.29 euros against a 52-week range of 36.17 to 63.94, a 50-day average of 38.98 and a 200-day of 45.82. The near-term trend has turned up; the medium-term trend has not.

## 4. THE FLOOR — the single most important verification, and it fails

Our board recorded a downside floor of 37.365 euros and a recovery risk-reward of 2.76 against a live price of 39.72. Both inputs are now stale in both directions. The floor was breached on the way down — the shares traded to 36.17 euros in the week to 27 July — and the price has since run to 41.29, so the recorded entry level is gone too. **A level the security has already traded through is not a floor. It is a recent price.**

Is there any real floor? There is asset backing, which is a different and weaker thing:

- **What supports the price.** The Tencent stake is liquid, marked daily, and worth about 51.30 euros per Prosus share against a 41.29-euro price. Prosus is also the dominant buyer of its own stock: the open-ended repurchase programme running since 27 June 2022 has returned close to 42 billion dollars and retired about 30% of the free float, and it is still running at scale — the 14 July 2026 update discloses 2,527,143 shares bought in the week of 6 to 10 July at an average of 39.5574 euros, roughly 100 million euros in five sessions. Buying back stock at a 37% discount lifts value per share by arithmetic every day the discount persists.
- **Why that is not a floor.** The support marks to market on a volatile foreign equity. If Tencent returns to its 52-week low of HK$411, about 8 euros per Prosus share of value simply disappears and the stock can trade to the mid-30s with the discount unchanged. There is no cash tender, no deal price, no net-cash backstop — net debt is 6.8 billion dollars, small at about 4% of the portfolio, but a liability rather than a cushion. A special-situation floor is a number somebody is contractually obliged to pay you. There is none here.

The defensible adverse case is therefore not 37.37 euros. It is Tencent retesting the low HK$400s with the unlisted book marked down for the same emerging-market risk aversion and the discount stuck near 37%, which puts Prosus at roughly **34 to 35 euros**.

## 5. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

**Concerning**

- The labelled catalyst is spent, and was never sized to matter — under 2% of asset value even before it resolved. What is left is a quarter of one percent of the share price, settling in late 2027.
- The recorded floor broke, and what sits beneath the price is Chinese-equity exposure, which is uncapped and unhedged in this book.
- The nine percent rally of the past week has taken the spread with it. Against our board's 46.21-euro target the upside is now about 12%, down from 22% a week ago, while the modelled downside is unchanged at roughly 16%. The setup has got worse, not better, precisely because it worked.
- One asset drives three-quarters of the value, and its next scheduled test is 12 August 2026, when Tencent reports second-quarter results. That is a real date, but it is two-sided and it belongs to another company.
- The holding-company discount is structural and has never durably closed. Morgan Stanley upgraded to overweight on 25 March 2026 with a 51-euro target, explicitly because the discount had reached the top of its range. Four months on the shares are still about 19% below that target and the discount is wider than when the call was made.
- The street cannot agree the discount is even wide. Goldman Sachs initiated at neutral on 4 June 2026 with a 41-euro target — a level the shares have now reached — describing the discount as 30% against a 40% historical average, that is, narrow rather than wide. The gap between the two houses is methodology, which makes "the discount is at its extreme" a contested claim rather than a fact.
- Goldman's specific worry is worth carrying: weaker cash flow from the operating businesses could force Prosus to keep selling Tencent shares to fund the buyback, shrinking the asset that provides the backing.
- The residual regulatory question — whether Brussels accepts a 2027 settlement against an 11 October 2026 deadline — is a small negative option, not a positive one.

**Encouraging**

- Management executed a mandated sale about as well as one can be executed: premiums on both placements, then a strategic exit at 41.50 euros. That is evidence about how they will handle the next forced decision.
- The operating businesses have stopped being a drag. The year to 31 March 2026 delivered about 12% revenue growth, ecosystem adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation up roughly 44%, free cash flow above 1.5 billion dollars, and profitability across all three regional ecosystems for the first time.
- The balance sheet is conservative: 6.8 billion dollars of net debt against a 164.9 billion dollar gross portfolio, roughly 4%, with 2027 maturities already refinanced.
- The buyback is large, verifiable week by week, and self-reinforcing while the discount is wide.
- Disclosure quality is unusually high for a holding company: the asset value and its components are published daily and can be checked against market marks, which is why the numbers in this dossier are assertions about arithmetic rather than estimates.

## 6. HIDDEN SIGNALS

Two things are worth noticing in how this played out. First, Prosus asked Brussels on 25 May 2026 to be released from the forced sale altogether, and settled for a two-month extension instead. That is a management team that knew it was selling into a weak print and tried to avoid it — creditable, and also a reminder that the April placement at 20 euros was a genuinely poor price relative to what arrived eight weeks later. Second, the 41.50-euro outcome was produced by a third party's strategic appetite, not by anything Prosus engineered. The good result here was substantially luck, and should not be extrapolated into a management skill premium when underwriting the next mandated sale.

A third observation belongs to this week specifically. The prior review of this name named a re-entry condition: Tencent reclaiming its 50-day average with Prosus holding above 36 euros. Both have now happened. It is worth being explicit that this does not resurrect the event thesis — it is a technical condition on a Chinese equity, and satisfying it tells you the tape has turned, not that a catalyst exists.

## 7. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Trajectory: stable. The operating businesses are improving and the capital return is disciplined, but neither changes what the security is — a discounted claim on Tencent with a portfolio attached.

The single thing the director must weigh before sizing: **this name does not belong in an event-driven book.** The event that got it here has resolved, it was never large enough to move this price, and what remains is a Chinese-internet exposure wearing a special-situation label. The value case is separately genuine — a 37% discount on the company's own daily numbers, liquid asset backing at 0.80 times the Tencent stake alone, and a very large buyer of its own stock — but it has to be underwritten as a discounted holding company carrying China risk, sized for that, and not as a defined-risk trade with a floor, because there is no floor. And the entry point is now materially worse than it was a week ago: the same 0.80 times Tencent backing, but with 12% of upside to target instead of 22%.

Moat is not a meaningful concept for a holding company: the operating quality sits inside Tencent and belongs to Tencent, not to Prosus. The structural risk to terminal value is Chinese regulatory and geopolitical, which is real, long-known, and manageable rather than newly deteriorating.
